utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the parties had reached an agreement on practical matters for next week, but I would just like to first -- for this week, but I'd like to first start with the videolink so to see that that's done as quickly as possible because we're always dependent on technical support. I'd like to verify first whether the videolink is functioning well. I see on my screen that at the far end the microphone would be not be activated. Now it is it on. I see it on my screen. Could the representative of the Registry at the other side of the videolink confirm that she hears me and that she sees me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours. I hereby confirm that we can hear you and we can see you from this side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we can hear you and we can see you. Could you tell us who is with you in the videolink room.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, apart from myself, there is the ITSS ICTY technician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness be escorted into your videolink room.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the next witness, no protective measures, would be Mr. Djuric.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for the witness to arrive. May I take it that the witness has been informed about the course of events during this videolink testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we explained him -- I explained him personally and my investigator met with him or called him yesterday and explained the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric, can you hear us and can you see us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you and I can see you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric, before you give evidence the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djuric. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric, questions will be put to you by Mr. Ivetic. You'll soon see him on your screen. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Djuric.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DJURIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would first ask that you repeat your full name slowly so that it is properly entered into the record.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DJURIC
utterances.text: Milenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And your last name?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DJURIC
utterances.text: Djuric.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you give a written statement to the Defence team for General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to take a look at 1D01760.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The letters are very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it possible to zoom in on the other end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's okay. Now I can see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us if you recognise the signature on the first page of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could now turn to the last page of the document, can you tell us, sir, whose signature appears on this page of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, does the date which is recorded herein correspond to your recollection of the date you would have signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DJURIC
utterances.text: I think that the date is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Subsequent to signing this statement, did you have a chance to read the same in full to determine if everything was correctly recorded therein?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so do you stand by everything as written in your statement as being accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, everything I stated is accurate and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I were to ask you the same questions today on the same matters as in your written statement, would your answers today be substantially the same as is written in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wouldn't change my statement. I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, you have taken a solemn declaration to tell the truth today. Does that mean that what is recorded in your statement is truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DJURIC
utterances.text: Looking from my point of view, everything is accurate. I stated what I know, what I experienced. I couldn't talk about the things that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you believe everything that you have spoken about to be truthful?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time we would tender 1D01760 as the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. MacDonald. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement receives number D927.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D927 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would read the public summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Milenko Djuric was born in Kotor Varos and is a permanent resident of Vrbanci village in Kotor Varos municipality. He lived in Rastik village from his birth to the beginning of the war. His village is situated next to a Muslim village called Vecici. Vecici had 30 houses and 700 to 800 residents, whereas his village had 30 houses and approximately 100 residents. He was mobilised on 10 May 1992 into the Territorial Defence and tasked with protecting the Rastik village. Rastik village was attacked on several occasions by the forces in Vecici and were thus forced to move out. The Muslims set up barricades in Vrbanci on several occasions and thus put the witness and other Serbs under complete blockade and isolation from Kotor Varos. On 24 July 1992, the witness was on his way to his barn when Muslim and Croat soldiers captured him. He was tied up and locked in a cellar of the house of Kasim Ilibic in Vecici where several other Serbs were held. They were tortured and subjected to physical and psychological abuse. Two other Serbs being held were killed. The ABiH forces in Vecici had around 500 to 600 men, not all of them wearing uniforms, but even those without uniforms were armed. At the beginning of November, these forces were ambushed by the Serb army, and the witness and other survivors were liberated. After the witness was liberated, he heard from neighbours that the local Serb population retaliated against the captured Muslim soldiers in Grabovica because of the crime they had committed against the local Serb population. They said that the Serb army was unable to prevent the revenge, and the mothers of killed Serb boys were the most aggressive. Your Honour, that completes the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric, on behalf of General Mladic and the rest of the Defence team, I thank you for your testimony. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. MacDonald. Mr. Djuric, you've been only four a very short time with us. Nevertheless, I would like to thank you for coming to the location where the videolink room is and for having --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and for having answered the questions that were put to you by Mr. Ivetic. Even if it was short, it doesn't mean that your testimony is that short because we have your written statement, which was admitted into evidence, and therefore even if there was not -- there were not a lot of words spoken today, nevertheless your statement is received and is in evidence before this Chamber. I'd like to thank you again very much, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I wonder if I may be excused, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness, which is a witness who will testify without protective measures. And Mr. Lukic, that would be Mr. Branko Beric?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for Mr. Beric to be escorted into the videolink room. Madam Registrar at the other side of the videolink, is the next witness ready to enter the videolink room?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honours. He is on his way. He is just walking a little bit slow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for him to enter that courtroom. Mr. Lukic, I abuse the time by reminding you that the Chamber expected you to give us further information as to the drafting and filing of expert reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that the witness entered the videolink room, and you prepare for it, Mr. ... Madam Registrar, I have some technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. Beric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently you can hear us. Can you see us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see you and I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Beric, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Beric. Please be seated. Mr. Beric, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll soon see him on your screen. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Beric.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please slowly tell us your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Branko Beric.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D1675.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beric, did you give a written statement to the General Mladic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you on the screen, you can see a document. Can you see a signature on the document, and do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: This is my personal signature. I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we go to the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sure. This is again my personal signature. I signed the document on the 26th of June, 2014.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the signature on the last page is also yours. When you -- or, rather, did you have an opportunity to read your statement and did you make sure that everything was recorded correctly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had just one little objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will make short pauses between your answers and my questions to allow the interpreter to interpret everything correctly. I don't want to confuse you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Please make sure that the interpretation is really correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is recorded in your statement, or rather what you stated to the best of your recollection, is it all accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: In essence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do so, Mr. Lukic, the witness, at page 9, line 24, said: "Yes, I just had one little objection." Was that objection attended to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that moment, I was switching in between channels, so I didn't hear him saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Beric, you heard Judge Moloto. He heard you say that you had a small objection to the statement. Did you really say that; and if you did, what did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: That I said that now, that I had an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: No, I only said that I would like to ask you to watch the interpretation, make sure that it is correct when I provide my answers. That's all I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there anything that you would like to correct in the statement or not, according to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1675 receives number D928.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D928 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would read statement summary of Mr. Beric and I will have several questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Branko Beric will testify about interethnic relationships in Prijedor before, during, and after the multi-party elections, emphasizing that personally he saw Muslim groups training for combat at Carakova village. He will describe how a mortar artillery piece exploded in the village due to improper use. Mr. Beric will recount that as early as February or March 1992, the Muslims started to move out women and children from Prijedor voluntarily and in an organised manner. He will also speak about individuals wearing sweat suits in Prijedor and its surroundings as a sign of membership in the Patriotic League; i.e., in the Muslim military formations. Branko Beric was assigned to the Territorial Defence Staff and the logistics base established by the SDS, which was headed by Major Kuruzovic. He will present information about the establishing of Trnopolje collection centre, about helping the Muslim population at Trnopolje, by providing accommodations, food, and medical aid. Mr. Beric will testify that no individuals were killed at Trnopolje and there was no machine-gun nests or barb wire. He will describe how Ms. Penny Marshall made the photograph by which she deceived the international public. He will testify that the population there was provided food by the ICRC and the municipal Red Cross. Branko Beric has information about the secret storages of medicines and other military medical supplies found at Kozarac which were indicative of preparations for the war. He will also describe some examples where he provided assistance to the Muslims at Trnopolje. And that was his statement summary. Now I have several questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, could I ask one question to the witness, Mr. Lukic. Witness, you gave a statement. That statement has been admitted into evidence. Do you remember when it was not that you signed the statement but that you gave the statement? Therefore, the day on which you were interviewed? When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the same day. Or perhaps a day or a couple of days earlier. I don't remember the date, but that's when I signed the statement. On the 26th of June, 2014.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that was almost immediately not more than a few days after you were interviewed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something like that, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beric, did you have an opportunity after the war to talk to your fellow citizens who were of Muslim ethnicity? Did you talk to them about why they called Trnopolje a camp?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: These are my friends, former and current. Large numbers of them, especially during the summer, during vacation time we meet up. We're happy to see each other. We have a drink together. We are delighted to see one another. Most often these people come from Sweden and other countries. During these conversations, some of these friends of mine -- I mean, regardless, we grew up together, we never paid attention to ethnic background. They told me that after interrogations in the camp, which nobody is denying, Omarska or Trnopolje -- no, sorry, Keraterm. When they came to the centre in Trnopolje, within a few days time, they would leave, go to third countries or go home. They had the feeling that they had come to the best hotel in the world, like the Hyatt hotel, compared to Omarska, the camp of Omarska, of course, if you compare that to the collection centre in Trnopolje. When during these conversations why is it that now some Muslims, after these unfortunate events, and often not those who were at the collection centre or reception centre, would say that they say honest people never said that. I said, "Why do you call the reception centre a camp?" Then they said to me that thanks to this statement, they were given major privileges in third countries as such. If they say that they were not in a camp, they would have less benefits and less privileges in third countries, and also when returning to their own places of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 8 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have that on our screens, paragraph 8, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say: "In Trnopolje, I also saw a large number of Muslims from Kozarac dressed in sweat suits, while they wore military-issue boots." Did you react in some way when you noticed that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Before this answer, I have to provide Their Honours with an explanation. Because I worked in the veterinary service, and for years everybody knew me all over Prijedor in each and every settlement, and when I'd come in the morning between 9.00 and 10.00, by 1.00 at the latest, since I was in charge of the medical unit, I brought in medicine and they had an infirmary of their own, a Muslim infirmary that was organised at the reception centre of Trnopolje. There was good doctors there and a colleague of mine, Hasa, a veterinarian, was also working there. I brought them whatever they needed. On one occasion, because there were thousands of people there at one point, and I would even bring them substances that would do away with the unpleasant smells. Everybody knew me, masses of people, when I'd come to that football pitch, and a lot of people would gather around me. For example, on such occasions, I happened to be a smoker, to this day, and I'd always have two packs on me, and I would always give them cigarettes. I knew lots of these young men and it was really hard for me. Nothing had happened. They came to the reception centre of their own free will. Of course, it was the safest for them there. This is what I'm trying to explain, paragraph 8. I noticed that many of them wore track suits and jeans, and they had military-issue boots as footwear. I advised them to throw away these military-issue boots anywhere and that it would be better for them to walk around barefooted, it was already summertime, because the police would come in and they would come looking for some people on the basis of testimonies provided in Omarska by their own people, and then they would take them to Omarska. And I didn't want these young men to suffer because they were so naive. They listened to what I said, and hundreds of them threw away these boots, military-issue boots. They walked around barefoot until they went to third countries. They freely moved about, they went for baths, they would find slippers or flip flops which they used until they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We need page 5 of your statement now, paragraph 23. Mr. Beric, in this paragraph, you are commenting upon the skinny Muslim from the photographs in Trnopolje. Do you know anything more about him? Can you tell us more about him? Do you know him? What can you tell us about him today?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I know quite a bit. First of all, this young man -- well, I was there in that period. I am saying that I was there briefly for a month, a month and a half, and after that I was sent to the front for some reason. Probably because I helped Muslims a lot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. You say you were there. Where were you? Is that paragraph 23 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reception centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is Trnopolje, not Omarska. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This young man was not at Trnopolje at the reception centre there, probably. I cannot say exactly whether he was in Omarska or Keraterm. And then after the interrogation, he was released. He was released to the Trnopolje reception centre, and from there he went to third countries very quickly because the International Red Cross organised transportation to third countries practically every day either on buses or trains or trucks. This young man was ill unfortunately even before the war. His own neighbours testified to that to this day. I must say that I'm sorry to have heard that he had died recently. I'm sorry that this lady journalist deceived the entire world because in Trnopolje there was never any barbed wire or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Just a minute. I asked you about this young man. The skinny young man. What do you know about him? Where is he from? What was his ailment? Do you know anything?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I do. As far as I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, let's first ask about the name of the person, whether the witness -- Do you know what the name of that, as you said, skinny person is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I cannot remember right now. I knew so many people. All over the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where exactly did he live? A village, what house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not tell you exactly now. Just roughly. Close to a hamlet, Sivci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed and tell us what you know more about this person, preferably what you personally observed and know of rather than what others told you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see that because already then when this was photographed I wasn't there. I was at the front line in Gradacac, even before that. But I can describe the place where this photomontage was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have that in your statement. You've already described that. Tell me, do you know what this young man's ailment was, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: From his neighbours and friends, Muslims and others, I heard that the young man had tuberculosis, even before the war. Whoever wanted to, perhaps the Prosecutor or somebody, could have found this documentation at the health centre in Prijedor even before the war, because you know that such illnesses were always filed in records.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 35 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we need page 6 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could also tell us where he met this person before the war. Could you tell us, Witness, how and when did you meet that person before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About a year before the war in our local infirmary that belonged to the Prijedor veterinary station, I was sent there to replace a colleague, a vet, who had gone to do his military service, so I knew that area too. We had different activities of prevention and cure. I know that when I went out on these prevention campaigns, when we vaccinated dogs in particular, I noticed a young man like that. I think that I saw him near this hamlet of Sivci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Everybody avoids such people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you didn't speak to him, but he looked like the one, if I understand you well, that you saw on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 35 of your statement, we're just going to focus briefly on Nusret Sivac, you said in this paragraph of your statement that he was never in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: May I say --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which period does this pertain to? When is it that you know that he was not there, and do you know when he left Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: First, could I just give an introduction?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I knew Nusret Sivac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please answer the question to start with. If there's any further explanation needed, Mr. Lukic will let you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. It is a well-known matter that Nusret Sivac was in the Omarska camp, and nobody is denying that. When he was released after having been interrogated at the Omarska camp, of course, at first they were all brought to the reception centre in Trnopolje. Nusret Sivac spent only one day free in the reception centre, and then he left, I don't know how. I don't know whether he walked or took a vehicle. It's not far away. He went home to Prijedor where he had a wife and son. It so happened that he was an exceptional personal friend of my niece and her husband.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness repeat the names of these persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please repeat the name -- names of the persons you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nusret Sivac was friends before the war with my niece and her husband, Mladen Vukajlovic and Vesna Selimbegovic Vukajlovic. He turned to them when he came home, and Mladen, as a matter of fact, when he said that he wanted to go to a third country, Mladen offered him money, and he said that there was no need for that. So then through them he asked my nephew, my oldest sister, Selimbegovic Ciro - unfortunately, he and his friend, Mile, they died after the war - and they drove him from Prijedor to Gradiska as requested. And this nephew of mine, because of his name and surname, risked his own life. And then after the war, Nusret Sivac, as he was promoting his business related to his book, he wrote the most terrible things about my nephew. He said the most terrible things. And he actually did him a favour driving him to Gradiska, risking his own life. People could have asked en route who you are, where are you coming from, and they could have all fared very badly. However, thank God everything ended well. May I add something to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't -- Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I think the witness asked you something --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and you didn't switch on your microphone when you responded. Please repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beric, just briefly, if you can, our time is running. What do you wish to add?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I can add something else. I don't understand -- many Muslims wrote books. He was one of them. But I don't understand how come that a person who was in Omarska all the time can describe Keraterm and the reception centre in Trnopolje and what was going on in town? Could he have possibly been in all those places at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, this was a question, and you're here to answer questions. I can't answer your question or anybody else in the courtroom. In any case, thank you, Mr. Beric. This is all we had for you at the moment. Thank you for providing your statement and thank you for answering our questions.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I would like to thank the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Traldi, wouldn't it be wise to take the break now, five minutes early, so that you can then finish your cross-examination in one -- or would you be finished in five minutes? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think I could use five minutes fairly efficiently, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll -- Mr. Beric, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Traldi. You will see him soon on your screen. Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Traldi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have a few questions about your responsibilities during the relevant period. First, you say at the end of your statement that you left Prijedor on the 28th of July, 1992, and went to the front at Gradacac. What unit were you a member of when you went to the front?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I was assigned to the 3rd Battalion when I arrived at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's the 3rd Battalion of the 43rd Motorised Brigade of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When were you mobilised into that unit?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: About a month or a month and a half following the attack on Prijedor. I was a member of the medical service in the logistics base before that. That was my specialty from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to try to get the chronology a little bit more precise. In your evidence, how long had you been a soldier in that battalion before you went to the front?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date when I joined the battalion. It was first the 7th Battalion and then it was renamed and became the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And turning to your work at the logistics base that you just mentioned in Cirkin Polje, who was your superior officer there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Slobodan Kuruzovic. He was the chief of that logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did you have a rank there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I was a foot soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mention in your statement that you had a driver. Why were you entitled to a driver?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because in peacetime and in wartime alike, every paramedic has a vehicle assigned to him and a driver. I was a paramedic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that logistics base, among other things, provided food and supplies to the VRS and to the police; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I don't remember whether supplies were provided to the police, but, yes, the VRS, because the VRS provided security for Trnopolje and the logistics base. I just happened to know that on one occasion when we received a large quantities of cigarettes, those cigarettes were distributed among the police as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As to Trnopolje, did you ever have any position at Trnopolje, any official position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: No. I would just go there every day, around 9.00 or between 9.00 and 12.00 or 9.00 and 1.00, and I inquired as to what they were missing, what they needed. Sometimes I would deliver some medical supplies that they needed. On one occasion, the most important thing for them was to have disinfectant for the toilet bowls. There were a lot of people there and there was foul smell there. I had a very good co-operation with their medical unit. There was a very good doctor and my colleague, Hasa. I had very good co-operation with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now there was a foul small, in part, because thousands of people were using the outdoor toilets that they'd dug there; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that as well. Thousands upon thousands. Some were in their vehicles, some in the school. Especially mothers and children were in the school because it was a good building. There was a big sports facility there, and that's where they were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you yourself were not present at Trnopolje or even in Prijedor municipality anymore when the journalists' visit to Trnopolje occurred; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: There were all sorts of journalists, you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I only saw --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you. The visit you refer to in your statement, that occurred after you had gone to the front at Gradacac; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: That female journalist who is the author of that video-clip or that photo featuring barbed wire, is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there. But I am familiar with the area where that photo was taken. That area is the same. It hasn't changed to this very day. There was never barbed wire there and the footprint of the area is only 2 square metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Similarly, you were never there when Nusret Sivac was there and you don't know how long he was in Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I don't know how long. A day, a couple of days, three days perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And when I say in your statement: "I state that there was no fence around the centre and that Nusret Sivac was never there," in fact, as you've testified today, you know he was there, and you've put in your statement and attested to this morning something that you know not to be the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I never stated that he had never been in Trnopolje. I only know that when he was released from Omarska, he spent a couple of days there, and from there, anybody could go wherever they wanted. The Red Cross was very efficient in organising departures to third countries. He went home and then my cousin -- by nephew took him, his wife, and their son to Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any way you can assist us where the witness, in the English version, is recorded as having said "Nusret Sivac was never there"? Is there any possibility that there is a language issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no language issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no language issue. Then I leave it you Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I note we're at the time for the break. Before we break, I'm just going to put to you that you've included something in your statement that you've testified today that you clearly know not to be the truth. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: It may have been a slip of the tongue. I know that all those were released from Omarska would end in Trnopolje first, and then they would go home, and then to third countries. It may have been a slip of the tongue. I may have misspoken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if the witness says that he -- Witness, if you say you may have misspoken, do you mean to say that Mr. Sivac did not go to Trnopolje, because today you told us that he would have been there if only for a couple of days. Is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, yes. This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in your statement, which you said you had reviewed and to which you attested today, we read: "I state that there was no fence around the centre and that Nusret Sivac was never there." But today you are telling us that he was there, though you do not know for how long.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my assumption about the reception centre in Trnopolje that there were people there who stayed for a month or 20 days, but there were also those who had been interrogated and released and then they would stay there only a day or a couple of days. That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People who stayed there in my mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you just don't know, if I understand you well, for how long Nusret Sivac would have been in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Mr. Beric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, if you are ready, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask now about your colleague, or your fellow veterinarian, Sead Sivac, who you mention in your statement. Were you two friends?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And about how old was he in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Much younger than me; 23, 24, or 25. He was a student first, and then he joined the army. I really don't know how old he was. We worked together for a year, and we had a good relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Have you seen him since the war?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all the unnecessary microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You know he was detained in Omarska in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I don't know that personally. I only heard about that. I personally didn't see him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What you heard is also that he was taken out of Omarska one night in the summer of 1992 and never returned; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I only heard that he had been in Omarska. Unfortunately, I have not seen him after the war. I don't know what his lot was. People say that he was killed. I suppose that if he were alive, I would have seen him. There's no reason for the two of us not to meet after the war. We had a good relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you testified earlier today that you thought people would suffer if they were sent to Omarska. That's because you knew the people detained there, like your friend Sead Sivac, were being detained in terrible, criminal conditions, that people were being beaten, that people were being killed; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I don't know that but I heard stories, and I also saw on TV, I heard the testimonies of the people who were charged with such misdeeds in Omarska. Nobody in Prijedor denies that that happened. We saw things on TV, we know that there were trials. It would be a sin for anybody to say that things like that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, just to be very specific. You testified on direct that you were concerned while you were at Trnopolje that people would suffer if they were sent to Omarska. You were aware at that time in the summer of 1992 already that serious crimes were being committed against the prisoners in that camp; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a technical problem. Could we try to restore the connection. I think ... for one second I thought we would have restored the connection, but it seems that it's gone again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] We're back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it seems that we're connected again. Could I just verify. First of all, I see that the far end microphone is switched off. Could that be switched on again. It is. The microphone is on now. Mr. Beric, can you now hear us again and can you see us again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And can you see us as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can see you personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'll repeat my last question. You testified on direct that you were concerned while you were at Trnopolje that people would suffer if they were sent to Omarska. You were aware at that time in the summer of 1992 already that serious crimes were being committed against the prisoners in Omarska camp; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I can't say that I was aware of crimes. I only knew that there was a camp and that the conditions were somewhat harsh. Nobody in Prijedor denies that it was a camp. It would be very sad if somebody denied that. As to what was going on there, I don't know. I was never there. But I did see video-clips. I know that there were trials. I know that people have been taken to task for the goings-on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, focusing very directly on what you knew in the summer of 1992, what made you think the conditions there were harsh?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Well, towards the end of my occasional visits to Trnopolje, some were already being released from the camp in Omarska and I could notice that they didn't look too good. They complained of the conditions. They suffered from dysentery. I helped many of them in the out patients clinic in Trnopolje. There was an acquaintance of mine, a neighbour, Alija, who had arrived completely naked. There were a lot of abandoned houses in Trnopolje. I took him to one of them where he found some clothes, some very new and clean and good clothes. He had arrived completely naked and he had dysentery, and based on that I could conclude that the conditions in Omarska were bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the houses that had been abandoned in Trnopolje village, they'd been abandoned by the Muslims who used to live there; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes. But they used them during the day. They would go to their houses, they would take baths, they would go to their gardens to pick vegetables. They also grilled chicken in the courtyards. So during the day they were in their houses but at night they would go to the reception centre where they felt safe and protected from groups of extremists that might appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now you testified you would be at the reception centre during the day. Were you ever there at night?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: No, never. Neither I nor my driver. Nor Kuruzovic or his driver or his security detail. Only during the day. Our task or, rather, his task was to drive supplies to our security detail --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: -- the supplies consisting of cigarettes and those men were guarding the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going ask you to focus carefully on my questions. I understand that you were never at Trnopolje at night, what you call a reception centre. How do you know whether Major Kuruzovic was there at night?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I am not sure that he was ever there. I'm not sure that he ever went there during the night at least while I was there, for one month and a half. I can't give you any guarantees about the period thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, you testified a moment ago that you were never there at night, nor Kuruzovic or his driver or his security detail. And what I'm suggesting to you is you don't know whether Major Kuruzovic was there at night or not because you yourself weren't there at night; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: You're not right. Because I added something and that was for as long as I was in Prijedor for a month and a half, I can give you my personal guarantee that he didn't go there during the night -- during that period of time, and then after I left perhaps they went there during the night, but I can't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, did you live in the same house as him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Would you -- would you spend every night his company.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: No, I went to my own apartment where I joined my family during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you have no idea where he was at night, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: No, you are right, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you testified a moment ago that Muslims in Trnopolje village used their houses during the day. In fact, Muslims in Trnopolje village would spend the day in the camp, just like they spent the night there; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Well, those whose houses were further away. But they were all acquaintances and friends. They therefore used the houses that were closer. That's where they would have baths. They would spend time there. In -- they grilled some ten lamb on Bajram, on their religious holiday. They even invited me. They had better food than the security detail. Every day --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: -- the International Red Cross and the Prijedor Red Cross branch prepared food for them in large cauldrons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We'll get to the Red Cross in a moment. While we're speaking of these houses, Major Kuruzovic also had a house near Trnopolje camp that he would use; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: While I was there, I know that him, his lads, and myself would sit down across the road from the school. There was a house there, and there were some wines. I don't know whether he used that house, whether he went there at night. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you say in your statement that you're quite sure that he never raped anyone. You're aware, aren't you, that the same trials that you discussed earlier have concluded that he repeatedly raped a woman over and over, brutally, during the summer of 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: To this very day, I never attended any trials, sir. This is the first time I am in a courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand that, sir. You testified earlier that you were aware of findings about Omarska. What I'm putting to you is you're also aware of this finding, that Major Kuruzovic had repeatedly raped this woman. I'm putting to you, to be very clear, that the findings have been this happened at night and, as you've just testified, you have no idea what he was doing at night. That's the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I can just say one thing. It just so happened -- I don't know whether he attended your trial? I wasn't following. Was he there? Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask to you answer my question.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what to answer. Knowing this charming gentleman, why would he have to do something like that? I just know when he was there during the day, masses of his students walked up to him and he did his very best to please them, and I don't think that such a charming gentleman would do that. And to do that, I mean, the hygienic conditions were not good either. He was a great gentleman, a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to turn now for a moment to the Cirkin Polje logistics base. You testified early that that base supplied the VRS. Now, the Chamber has received evidence, P7129, about a meeting of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality and the garrison command on the 10th of June that Major Kuruzovic, and your colleague, Mirko Mudrinic, among others, attended and at which "all instructions given by the garrison command and the Crisis Staff in relation to the transformation of the Territorial Defence into the Army of the Serbian Republic of BH were accepted." Were you aware of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, P7129, is that under seal, and does that in any way needs to be addressed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It is for a different reason. It was used in -- it was used in open session placed, placed under seal because of a particular very specific piece of information that's not included in what mentioned just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, under those circumstances, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you recall the meeting on the 10th of June that I described a moment ago. Were you aware of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But you know the garrison command refers to the command of the 43rd Motorised Brigade of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I was an ordinary soldier. Nobody invited me to such meetings. I don't know what this is about. Maybe you could explain something to me and then I would know what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Witness, you just have to answer the questions to the best of your knowledge. That's everything you should do. You don't have to bother about background or whatever. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Beric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know of any such meeting, and I don't remember that, and it was probably the higher command that had a meeting. I have nothing to do with any of that, and I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you cannot answer a question, listen to the question and then tell us, I don't know. Carefully listen to the question. Mr. Traldi will now resume. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you testified earlier that Trnopolje was secured by the VRS. That was the 43rd Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: While I was there, it was the logistics base of the TO, and then later it was probably attached to the 43rd Motorised Brigade. At that moment, I was sent off to the front. They chased me away. Probably somebody didn't like the fact that I was helping Muslims a lot there at the reception centre. I brought them food and cigarettes, socialised with them, because they were all my acquaintances, and probably somebody was bothered by the fact that I was that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 20 of the statement of this gentleman, it was described who guarded, and it says that it was -- that it was reserve component of the army and they belonged to TO, Territorial Defence, organised by Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And at --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And at temporary transcript page 23, line 1, today, it was the testimony that I referred to, the witness said: "Yes, the VRS, because the VRS provided security for Trnopolje..." And then his sentence continued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you intervene on a matter of substance, you should, first of all, ensure that the witness cannot hear us. Therefore, apart from that you can deal with that in re-examination. But the mere fact that the witness has told something in the statement as recorded, as we all know by now doesn't mean that there's no need to put further questions on the matter to the witness. Therefore, Mr. Traldi may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 19152. And the Registrar received two sets of documents for this witness. This is part of the additional documents provided over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a report from Prijedor SJB Chief Simo Drljaca to CSB Banja Luka. Can you just say "yes" when you are able to see it on the screen there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Security station, Prijedor, CSB Banja Luka, chief dispatch, your dispatch number such and such --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I am going to interrupt you. I'm not requesting that you read the whole document. If I could direct your attention to the third paragraph, we see Chief Drljaca refer to what he describes as an open reception centre in Trnopolje, and looking at the final paragraph, he writes: "This centre is secured by the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and he says: "No investigation activities are carried out in it." Now that's consistent with your testimony earlier today, though not with your statement, that it was the VRS that secured Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: That's a mistake on his part. That's a mistake on his part. Can I just see what the date is?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You can see it in the top left: The 9th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Until then it was the Territorial Defence because by that date I was not in Trnopolje in the logistics base. I was already at the front line. Now whether it became the VRS then -- but until then, I know for sure that it was the Territorial Defence and things changed every day. One platoon from each local commune, usually it was elderly people -- it was a mix of people but usually elderly people from the Territorial Defence. Now after this date it is possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you there. I'd tender the document and then I will have a follow-up question about your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The number, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 19152 receives number P7197.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the 65 ter number, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 19152, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The record is complete now. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, in fact, security at Trnopolje was provided by the TO for only a few days and then it was taken over by the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Not a few days. Roughly a month and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's see 65 ter 32239, page 60. This will be a portion of Mr. Kuruzovic's testimony in the Stakic case. And I'm looking at the bottom of the page at line 20. And he's asked by Mr. Stakic's counsel: "Is it correct that only for the first few day, the security was provided by people from the Territorial Defence? He answers: "Yes, that is correct." Mr. Stakic's counsel asks him: "After a few days, the security was provided by the 43rd brigade?" And he responds: "Yes, I don't know when this happened, whether it was after two or three days, but very quickly after that, there were already a number of people. The security had to be stepped up." And he explains why. Now, that, what you're superior officer, Major Kuruzovic, testified, that's the truth, that beginning just a few days after it opened, security at Trnopolje was provided by the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Am I supposed to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Possibly. But, still, I saw the same people who were changing there every day. The same people, same uniforms. Now whether they were renamed into something different, that I don't know. I just know that while I was there, it was always the same people and they took turns. These platoons that used to belong to the TO. Now if somebody included them in the VRS, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32006.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As it comes up, we saw in that last answer that Major Kuruzovic said security had to be stepped up a few days after the camp opened. Were you working at Trnopolje at the end of May 1992 or visiting Trnopolje at the end of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I think I came in May. I think I was still coming in May. I still hadn't been chased away to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a Croatian intercept from a few days after the camp opened; 31 May 1992. We read that there is a collection centre for non-Serbs at the stadium in Trnopolje village. And the Croatians write that: "The enemy is concerned about a breakout from the camp or escape, so an order has been issued to strengthen security, if necessary, to three times what it was." Now that's just about exactly the time that Major Kuruzovic was saying secured needed to be stepped up; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, could you repeat your last answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unnecessary microphones pleased be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly. I don't know. I just know that there were no escapes. Nobody escaped. Nobody was running away from the reception centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you would only be concerned about escapes or the possibility of a breakout if the people there were detained; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Not necessarily. Maybe somebody would escape to join their forces, their army. In other places there were still a Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you is you only escape from detention. If you're free to go, you just walk away. You're using the word "escape" because these people were prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: No. Because during the day, they could go wherever they wanted to and at night-time, when there was a curfew, nobody was allowed to move about, Serbs included. When there's a curfew, you know that in any war, there's a curfew. During the day, as a matter of fact, I and my driver drove a colleague of his to Prijedor to see his girlfriend, to take a shower, because it was safer for him to spend the night at the reception ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 32006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We object to these type of documents, as always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any specifics for this one or just in more general terms that you oppose the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We always -- there is no, as I remember, audio recording, and it's not -- there's no source on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I take it it's from a series, Mr. Traldi, or could you say a little bit more about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's correct. It's from a lengthy series.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it's in indirect speech. There is no concrete words. Somebody told us a story about something he thinks he saw -- heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We're not seeking to attribute speech to any particular individual. So while that might go to weight, I don't see how it would relate to the admissibility of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it's an intercept and does not -- is not attributed to anybody, I don't know how that could be intercept at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, sometimes even not knowing who the interlocutors are, you can intercept a conversation. You can overhear a conversation sometimes without knowing exactly who is speaking, Mr. Lukic. That's not new to you, is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But in this intercept it does not say that they did not know who or that they had any kind of problems identifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think Mr. Lukic will be familiar with this collection containing a number of summaries, not all of which refer to the speakers explicitly by name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, the document will be marked for identification. The Chamber wants to take a bit more time to find exactly which series it comes from, et cetera, and where it -- what decisions we took for intercepts of the same series.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I can provide additional information. I would have to do it in private session, so I'd suggest we do it at the break, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take that you have done with the document so we can do that at a later stage --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Lukic. Madam Registrar, the number under which this document will be MFI'd is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number is P7198.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, can we please have 65 ter 31654.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a report on the work of the Prijedor municipal organisation of the Red Cross from the 5th of May to the 30th of September, 1992. If we turn to page 9 in the English, 8 in the B/C/S, we see a number of points below comment -- or below conclusion and comment. The last of them is that: "23.000 people have been housed through the reception centre at Trnopolje, of whom we and the International Red Cross have dispatched 1.561 to the Karlovac reception centre. On 29 September 1992, a convoy was escorted to Karlovac in the presence of European observers." Now, this reflects what you've testified about already today, that there were many, many thousands of people who went through Trnopolje in the summer of 1992 and many of them were sent to third countries on convoys; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the people at Trnopolje, they were Muslims and Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember. Perhaps there were a few Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the rest, Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And they were civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Including women, children, and elderly people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Including people who were civilians, conditionally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The people there that were civilians that were Muslims and a few Croats, they included women, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: They included children, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And they included elderly people; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 65 ter 31654.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 31654 receives number P7199.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now can the Prosecution please have 65 ter 07021b.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a report on the CSCE mission to inspect places of detention in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If we turn to page 4 in both languages, we see a memorandum on Trnopolje. Looking at the second paragraph, we see that at the time this was drafted, "the number of inmates at the centre, of whom the great majority, if not all, are of the Muslim faith, is currently thought to be in the neighbourhood of 2.000." It says: "These people are living in terror and the CSCE mission believe they have substantial reasons for their fears." Now they were living in terror because of the conditions in Trnopolje camp; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Well, my family lived in fear at home too. And I'm angry about what is written here, "camp." Please, it was a reception centre, not a camp. I know that in English everything is "kamp," but it is a reception centre, not a camp, and I don't allow that. I won't allow it to be written, "camp."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please refrain from telling what other people should do, and would you please just answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to repeat my question. The people were living in terror because of the conditions in Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: My family at home lived in fear too because of the civil war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, do I understand that you accept that people were living in fear in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably. There was a war going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you accept that it was due to the conditions in Trnopolje? Apart from there being a war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sanitary conditions were difficult, but they had better food than the people who were guarding them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender 65 ter 07021b.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 07021b receives number P7200.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Continuing with the topic of international observation for a moment, in paragraph 22 of your statement, you say the International Red Cross was present at Trnopolje from day one. In fact, it was the Bosnian Serb Red Cross that was present early in Trnopolje's existence; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, a lady from the International Red Cross came and she was there from day two or three, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: And they provided food every day for those who were there. It was cooked every day and brought in huge cauldrons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- what I'm putting to you is that it was not the Bosnian Serb -- or the International Red Cross. It was not the International Red Cross that was present early in Trnopolje's existence. It was the Bosnian Serb Red Cross; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I think you could have checked that with the Red Cross. There was a lady from the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, I asked because the Trial Chamber's received, for instance, P3965, a document from the International Red Cross that reflects that they were first able to enter Trnopolje around the 10th of August, 1992, after you'd left. So I'd put to you that it was, in fact, the Bosnian Serb Red Cross, not the International Red Cross, and you are mistaken.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I claim that that lady was from the International Red Cross. She compiled a list of those who wanted to leave. None of us from the logistics base ever compiled any lists. It was her in co-operation with the Prijedor Red Cross. On a daily basis, she compiled lists of those who wanted to go to third countries, and they did leave in cars, lorries, buses. I don't know who it -- who else it was who compiled lists of those who wanted to leave, and those lists were forwarded a couple of days after they were compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Those people who left, they left on convoys, and the Prijedor police and the VRS assisted in organising and securing those convoys; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, the reserve police. At first I know that they were headed for Novska, in Croatia. Most of them were, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now I'm going focus on the conditions at Trnopolje for a moment. You're aware that many prisoners slept outside; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: How could they be prisoners if they slept outside? It is correct that they did not sleep inside because there was not enough room. They slept in their vehicles, tractors, lorries, those that they had arrived in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But not in their homes because those had, in many cases, been destroyed by Bosnian Serb forces; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: You are partly right. They did not sleep in their homes because they were safer in the reception centre. Their houses were not destroyed then. It happened only later or after the war. Their houses were not destroyed because the Serbs who had been expelled from Bosanska Kladusa arrived and settled in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, for instance, in Kozarac, the Chamber has received evidence from a number of Defence witnesses as well as Prosecution witnesses about the destruction of homes there. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes. A large number was destroyed. Not all. A lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you claim in your statement: "In the period while I was in Trnopolje, no one even suffered as much as ear pulling." Now, the Chamber has received evidence that several Muslims in Trnopolje were taken out of Trnopolje were murdered. Is it your evidence you weren't aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I don't know that they were murdered. I know that from time to time the reserve police came with an order to investigate some of the Muslims in Trnopolje and took statements from them. They had orders to take some Muslims and take them to Omarska. I don't know whether they took them there or somewhere else. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, Slavko Puhalic testified recently. He described himself as the link between Major Kuruzovic and the other men. He was essentially Kuruzovic's deputy; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he was, whether he was his deputy. I know that he was the one who spent most time in Trnopolje so he knows much more than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
