utterances.text: Well, he testified that he was aware Muslims had been taken out and killed. Is it your evidence that neither Major Kuruzovic nor any of your other co-workers at the logistics base had informed you that Muslims had been taken out of Trnopolje and killed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Nobody ever told me that. And what I've just told you was that at the moment I was there, the police did arrive in a blue van. They had a written order to take some people to Omarska. I don't know whether they indeed took them to Omarska or somewhere else. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And none of the prisoners you spoke with ever told you that people had been taken out and murdered. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: No. My Muslim acquaintances with whom I spoke on a daily basis did tell me that people were taken away, but they never told me that anybody was murdered. How could they have known? People were taken -- or they left and then their friends and acquaintances would drive them all the way to the Croatian border.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you know that people were being taken away from Trnopolje that never came back; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I really don't know whether anybody returned or not. There were thousands upon thousands of people there. How should I know if some of them returned?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Chamber has received evidence that there were numbers of rapes not just by Major Kuruzovic but large numbers of rapes in Trnopolje camp, and again Slavko Puhalic testified that he was aware of some of them. Is it your evidence you never heard from Major Kuruzovic or anyone else that people were being raped in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: While I there, I did not hear any such thing. I didn't hear that. Possibly during the night when we were not there. Slavko perhaps knows because he was there more often and stayed longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Witness, could I ask you one question. You said you know that the police was taken persons and you don't know whether they took them to Omarska or somewhere else. You don't know. Do you know whether they were returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if the police would have taken someone, you wouldn't know whether they were returned by the civilian police who had led them away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I put to you your statement in paragraph 33, which reads: "There were cases when the civilian police took some individuals for interrogation to Omarska, but all of them returned to the Trnopolje reception centre after interrogation." This squarely contradicts what you said a minute ago, that you do not know whether they were returned. Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I firmly answer, and I speak the truth: I never stated that they were brought back, that they returned. I never stated that. I claim categorically, I know it personally, I was present when the police brought an order to Kuruzovic and when they took those people away. I never said it in any statement. I never stated that they returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I read your own statement to which you attested today that it was, after you had reviewed it, it was the truth --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have misspoken. Let me see if I can find this and read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph 33, could it be shown to the witness. But I'm not engaging in a debate on the matter, Witness. I just wanted to draw your attention to the fact that your statement says something which is squarely contradicting to your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that I ever stated that they were brought back. It may have been a -- a slip of the tongue or a misprint. I -- I continue to claim that they were taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, are you aware that today you told us that you had reviewed the statement and that you attested that what you said was reflected well and that you attested that you gave your statement in accordance with the truth and that is what you told us today before we admitted into evidence that statement. When you say it may have been a slip of the tongue, do you mean to say that it's not all the truth, what is in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just flipped through my statement, and while I was doing that, I -- maybe I didn't not notice that. I claim that they were taken away, but I did not state that they were brought back. Some may have been brought back. I don't know whether all were. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you say that you have not carefully read and reviewed your statement before you gave you're attestation today, that it was all in accordance with the truth and well recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I was saying, because - because - I thought that we would slowly go through the paragraphs in my statement one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that expectation was not accurate. I don't know on what it is based, but Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, is it your evidence that when -- is it your evidence now that when Mr. Lukic asked you at temporary transcript page 9, beginning at line 21: "When you -- or, rather, did you have an opportunity to read your statement and did you make sure that everything was recorded correctly? You answered: "Yes, I just had one little objection," which you later explained was about ensuring the translation was correct. Is it your evidence now that your answer to that question was not, in fact, the truth, that you did not read your statement and make sure everything was recorded correctly in advance of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the session, at the -- counsel said that there was an objection. I thought that that had been corrected, and it seems that it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You were asked what the objection was. You told this Court that you'd asked that it be made certain that the interpretation was correct and then swore to your statement. You swore to a statement that you did not know to be true and that you've now today said contains a number of errors, and you swore that you'd reviewed it and made sure it was correct when the truth is you did neither of those things. Right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I've never been at a trial before, and I thought that you would go through the statement paragraph by paragraph, and then I would be asked to say whether something was correct or not. This is my first trial ever, so I thought that what mattered was what you were going ask me, what the Presiding Judge would ask me, what the Defence counsel would ask me. I thought that that was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: For the moment I'd just ask for an answer to the question I just asked you, which is that when you testified under oath that you'd reviewed your statement and made sure what was in it was true, in fact, you had not done either of those things; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not that nothing is correct, but what we are looking at now, i.e., that they were brought back, I don't know about that. I'm sure, and I still claim, that they were taken away, but I don't think that I ever said that they were brought back. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we are at or even slightly past the time for the break. I'd appreciate having it to reorganise. I imagine I'll be very brief after it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll take the break now for 20 minutes, and we'll resume at 25 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, after reviewing over the break, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Lukic, any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will have several questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Beric, you were asked earlier today about the logistics base. I would like to call up 07157.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that a P number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, it's not P number, it's 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beric, this is a report on the work of the logistics base. The date is 16 September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at the following page, please, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, you can see --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, we don't have that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, this is for re-direct. We did not send it. But I can ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Beric, do you know who Mirko Mudrinic was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was his position at the logistics base; do you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: He was an organiser in the logistics base. He did have a rank, but I can't remember what it was. I believe that he was Kuruzovic's assistant more than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're saying that he was an organiser. Did you co-operate with him at the logistics base?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: As needed. If I needed some medical supplies or foodstuffs at the logistics base, he was the one who was involved in all that more than anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In today's transcript, it was recorded when you testified about your friend Alija who had arrived from Omarska. It was recorded that he was stark naked. Did you say that he was naked or stark naked?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: He was almost naked. The only thing he had on him were very dirty underpants.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you talk to Kuruzovic and his escorts while you were sitting in the shade of wine, as you put it? Did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In those conversations, did anybody mention that Kuruzovic visited Trnopolje during the night?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, did any of the people you spoke to, Muslims or Serbs, complain about Kuruzovic? Did anybody say that Kuruzovic had ever raped anybody?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at P7199. I don't know if the representative of the Registry can call up that number. The former 65 ter number was 31654. This is a report on the work of the municipal Red Cross branch in Prijedor from 5 May to 30 September 1992. We need page 9 in English and page 8 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Talking about this document, you were asked whether there were any women and children there, whether there were elderly people as well. Now those children, those women and those elderly, were they brought in, as far as you know, or did they come of their own will? Did they actually ask to be accommodated there? How did these people arrive in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: They came on their own using all sorts of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The last part of your question is is how the question should have been formulated. The previous part is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Separately, I'm not entirely sure that the question about how they arrived arises out of my cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Still, we think it's very important to establish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- it was established --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- that there were elderly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But not by providing an answer before you ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, matters may be important, but the issue raised by Mr. Traldi, whether it arises from cross-examination, it does not. If you say were there any red-haired people there, and to say, Well, then we have to know everything about red-haired people. That, of course, is not touched upon how they arrived by Mr. Traldi, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. But if it's not in dispute, or they claim that they that were forced, if they claim they were incarcerated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- they had to be brought there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we are not dealing with one witness only. I think that the Prosecution's case in that respect is very clear. If you only listen to the questions, you know that it is in dispute perhaps, but the arrival, as such, was not addressed in cross-examination. At the same time, it may take more time if you have one or two questions on this, I would say, it's more practical to do that, but from a procedural, legal point of view, you are not entitled to what I allow you, nevertheless, to do at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then also please be precise in terms of avoiding sweeping statements, because that is of some concern to the Chamber in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Beric, do you know anything specific or do you know anybody specific and how they arrived in Trnopolje reception centre?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I know a lot about that. Many came on foot from Prijedor. And they continued taking food to their relatives in Prijedor and they returned. And I also know that they came in various vehicles. They used taxis. They paid the fare. There were taxis during the war as well. And they arrived because they had heard that their departure to a third country would happen fast. There was a neighbour of mine and her two daughters, Ramiza and her daughters Anita and Rita, who paid the taxi fare and arrived at the reception centre. When I appeared there around 9.00 or 10.00 and when I saw them, I was taken by surprise. She toured the reception centre and realised that the conditions would be much better there for her children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One simple question for you, Witness. Did it ever happen that people arrived being accompanied by either police or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Prijedor, as far as I know, people came of their own will, on foot or by taxi, or by their own vehicle. I remember just one case when Muslims were collected in Sanski Most and brought over by lorries, and those people left on the same day by train. They were escorted either by the police or the military. I don't know who. I can't remember. But in any case, a convoy was organised for them on the same day and they left by train.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you ever present when people arrived from Omarska and Keraterm escorted by the police; do you remember if any such thing happened while you were there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were at Trnopolje, was anybody brought from Omarska or Keraterm escorted by the police?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Those who had been interrogated and were let go came by buses. I suppose that they had escorts. I didn't see them. They had been interrogated and released and they arrived, and from Trnopolje they were sent to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I call up P7200.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Can I finish what I started telling about my neighbour?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is in your statement, so there's no need to repeat anything from your statement.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need P7200. I don't know if the representative of the Registry can find this document. It used to be 07021b, 65 ter. This is a report issued by the CSCE mission about detention centres in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We need to look at page 4 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beric, in the second paragraph, line 2, you will see where it says -- in English, it is line 3. It says: "These people are living in terror and the CSCE mission believe they have substantial reasons for their fear." You told us that your family lived in fear in Prijedor as well. My question to you is this: Your conduct and the conduct of the armed Serbs who were there contributed to the fear of those people. Why were they afraid? What was the cause of their fear?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: You know what the reason was? There was a civil war going on and it's only natural that everybody should feel afraid. There is fear in everyone. There is poverty, hunger, there is no electricity. Any normal person would try to avoid that. All of us were hungry, without electricity, and we were wondering what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question in relation to today's paragraph -- no, today's transcript, page 46, line 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Traldi asked you about the people who were leaving. "... they were leaving on convoys, and the Prijedor police and the VRS assisted them in organising and securing these convoys; right?" And in your answer you said: "Yes, the reserve police." Do you have any knowledge about the VRS, whether the VRS ever escorted these convoys?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that because very soon I was sent to the front line. I know that up until then, it was the police that was securing convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Beric. That's all we had for you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Beric, I have -- before I give an opportunity to the Prosecution to put any further questions to you. In your statement you are telling that you claim that Sejmenovic is not telling the truth about his stay at Trnopolje, as you said, because you know him personally. How do you know what Sejmenovic told this Court about Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I heard about that. I heard about that from other people. I didn't personally watch his testimony in court, but that's something that I heard from other people. However, I can tell you about how come we know each other and how everything happened and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not interested in that. I'm primarily interested in how you knew what he had told the Court. So you haven't watched any testimony given by him? You have not read any of his statements?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You -- you did not read those statements. Did you speak to him personally about his testimony in this Court?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I didn't talk to him about the testimony. We didn't see each other. We're good acquaintances, friends. Sivac was his best friend and he often came to see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whether what he told this Court is the truth or not, you've got no idea because you don't know what he told this Court?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I'd like to know what it was that he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine, but you commented on it already without knowing what it was. I have no further questions in relation to that. Are you -- Nusret Sivac, do you know whether and, if so, what evidence he gave to this Court?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't watch it directly. I just know what he wrote in the book. And he turned it into a business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Beric, earlier today, you said - and this is on page 16, line 13 and 14 - you talked about this skinny man which was -- who was depicted in this photograph we talked about. And you said: "I must say, that I'm sorry to have heard that he died recently." When did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: A few days ago. A few days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what did you hear precisely? When did he die?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Well, allegedly, it was recent. The last couple of months or something. I have no idea. I heard that from the neighbours out there. Now whether it's true, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "the neighbours out there"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: Well, people who live in the nearby villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you hear that in the street or by -- in a cafe or did anybody specifically tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BERIC
utterances.text: In the street. You know what it's like. People live together again. What happened, happened. People co-operate. They work together, Muslims and Serbs, and every day there are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Beric, this concludes your evidence in this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to the place of the -- the location of the videolink. I also thank you for having answered questions that were put to you by the parties and put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are excused. Madam Registrar, at the other side of the videolink, is there any -- perhaps we first allow the witness to leave the videolink room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber was informed that the next witness would not be available. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next witness from yesterday would be available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the next witness for the videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next witness for the videolink, we could not anticipate that we would finish this early so we called only those two for today for videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that means that he is expected to start his testimony tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar at the other side of the videolink, we do understand that there's no witness available at this moment to continue hearing evidence through this videolink but that we would resume tomorrow morning. Is that the same information that you have?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, at this moment, we can close the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honours next videolink witness -- the next one is ready for tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 not in this -- yes, for you in that same courtroom through videolink.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we can close the videolink for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we can continue the cross-examination of the last witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before it gets lost if we could handle the matter regarding MFI P7198.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd ask that we move into private session for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic, an update on, I think, five expert reports. Two ballistics, one historical, one forensic pathologist, and one radio communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We hope that ballistics experts could be finally filed by the end of the next week. And we are awaiting the translations for historical expert and pathologist. Hopefully tomorrow it could be -- we hope that tomorrow that this pathologist expertise could translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you provided the original versions already to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Hmm? Maybe Ms. Stewart knows, because it's up to our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you send them for translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That I don't know. Tomorrow one should be done probably a couple of weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Isn't it that you would always provide the original versions to the other party already since you are so much in delay?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd been standing up. None of us had recalled seeing them, and I was just going ask to assist us in checking our records for the names of the witnesses that Mr. Lukic had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if not, we'll send it today, I promise that. And on the 18th of March, the translation for historian expert should be finalised [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have the names of your experts? Or if you would send an e-mail to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Pathologist is Dunjic. I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I'm a bit concerned if I hear that possibly you have not given the original versions, and I think that it was what was as a provisional remedy agreed upon, that at least if you have any report ready awaiting translation that you already send the original to the Prosecution to the -- and if that doesn't happen, then -- it doesn't take that much time, I would think. It requires some attention to what is done. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I didn't hear any update on the radio communications expert. We had asked the Defence if they objected to us a short interview of such an expert to get an idea of what he may be testifying about, and we await your reply on that, and especially that we haven't seen any report or any word of any report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you ask to have an opportunity to interview the expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it was a week or two ago, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Friday two weeks ago or last Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My recollection is last Friday since I spoke with Mr. McCloskey on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objection against ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It hasn't been resolved because we have not received word back from the communications expert, and we also have not received his report, although that the Belgrade office tells me that they expect his report to be done by next week, and then it can be sent for translation. As soon as we get the B/C/S report, we can provide that to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the question also was whether the Prosecution could interview that expert. Apparently that's how I understood your request to the Defence as expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I transferred that request to Belgrade to communicate to the radio communications expert. I have not heard back in relation to that, and I don't know that my colleagues have either. I think looking back here, they have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it the expert who decides on that or is it the Defence who approves an interview? And is there any property in a witness? That's, of course, the question that arises. Mr. Ivetic, it's not the expert who -- you were asked whether you oppose your expert to be interviewed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I relayed that request to my lead counsel, Your Honour. I can't speak with authority on matters that I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then ask now your lead counsel what his position is. He is sitting next to you, so communication shouldn't be a major problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The instructions I'm getting in the courtroom right now are that as far as we're concerned we don't have a problem with the proposal, but we can't speak on behalf of the witness since we have not heard back since we communicated that request to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you're willing to give the details for communication to the Prosecution so that they can approach him?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They should already have that, but I can check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that will be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then there's one other matter remaining; that is, we were informed that the parties had agreed on how to proceed this week. I don't know whether that is covered by the information that Mr. Subotic would resume his testimony today and that after the videolink, then if it has not been finished, we would continue with, if I could say, The Hague witnesses. Is that your agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is, Your Honours, and that is the preliminary matter that we were ready to raise before which delayed to have the videolink start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Then I suggest that we ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That we take a break now, that we will resume at 25 minutes past 1.00, and that we'll then further hear the testimony of Mr. Subotic. We take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll now continue with hearing the evidence of Mr. Subotic. Could he be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If my recollection serves me well, we're about to start the cross-examination. That's where we are. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd first like to explain to you why you are with us in court only today again for a relatively short period of time. That is because we also hear evidence from witnesses who are far away, we hear them through a videolink, and for the technical requirements we unfortunately have to give priority to that, which then may not be very pleasant for you. I hope you have some understanding for that. Mr. Subotic, I'd first like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And I then inform you that you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Hasan. You'll find Ms. Hasan to your right. Ms. Hasan is counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Hasan, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your commander, Major Zoran Malinic, what was he commonly known as? What was his nickname?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Zoran Zoka. That's the usual way in which Zorans are addressed. We addressed him by rank, we, the soldiers. And then there were friends of his who would come to see him. Zoki, Zole, Zoka. So that's the usual nicknames for that particular name.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now you recall testifying yesterday about Muslims who were killing other Muslims that wanted to surrender. And what I'd like to ask you is did you report that information that you received to your commander, Malinic?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through some report everyday; that is to say, every time I went out on patrol and when I'd come back, every time a report is filed, an Official Note, and at the same time I inform the commander. And this was very fast, everything that happened at the stadium. I received this information and the people who had been taken prisoner said that that had happened. I could not confirm that to him because I didn't see that myself, what it was that had happened. What happened to these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Besides filing official reports, or notes as you mention, you kept Zoran Malinic informed of what was transpiring?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that day we saw each other about two or three time, and it had to do with radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you made -- you made Zoran Malinic aware that there were wounded amongst the prisoners who surrendered, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said that to Petrovic because I asked him for a vehicle. Malinic hadn't appeared by then. Well, maybe he did, but I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's take a look at P1415. What you're about to see is an intercepted communication. It's from the 13th of July at 10.09 hours in the morning. And I'm not going to work through the entire communication, but it begins between Beara and Lucic and then continues between a Zoka and Beara. And it's -- we can turn in the English to page 2. And it's our position that Zoka is Zoran Malinic, commander of the military police of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. And the part of the conversation I want to focus on is the -- when Zoka gets on the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 5 in the B/C/S, please. And if we can look at -- you see towards the bottom there, you see 500. If we can just turn the page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And just towards the top of the page there in the English, Zoka reports to Beara that there are about 500.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we turn the B/C/S one page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And Zoka says, just a little bit further down in the English: "Well, here, it's ... they're killing themselves ... there are also plenty of wounded ..." And I believe we have to turn to page 7 in the B/C/S. And Beara says: "You mean they're doing it amongst themselves?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, the conversation continues, but it's not heard very well what Zoka says. And then Zoka says: "... they're killing...." Beara says: "Well, excellent. Just let them continue, fuck it." You see that?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And that information that Zoka is passing onto Beara accurately reflects what was taking place at the time and what had you reported to Malinic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see that this is Malinic. Zoka can be whoever. I did report to my commander via radio communication that I had come across this group of people who had unfortunately been killed, whatever else happened, but I did not report to him about anything else. And who this was that was talking to Beara, I really cannot say to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm going to tell you that there's evidence in this days that Malinic who -- testified that he spoke to Beara on the 13th of July at about 10.15 in the morning. And so I'll ask you again: The information that is Zoran Malinic is providing to Beara is, in fact, what you had testified to yesterday, was it not?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's a coincidence. I don't know what my commander had to say to the chief of security and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. By approximately 2.00 p.m. that day, there were more than a thousand people at the football stadium at Nova Kasaba; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something like that. About a thousand or 11- or 1200, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And Muslim men continued to surrender after that time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- most surrendered in the morning before noon and later they surrendered in groups of five or ten. In smaller numbers. The larger contingent of those who surrendered, some 2- or 300 of them, surrendered during the morning before 1.00 or half past 1.00. I can't remember exactly, but that was approximately the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, sir, by the afternoon around 4.00 p.m., 5.00 p.m., you wouldn't dispute that there were approximately 1500 prisoners gathered at that stadium, would you?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "1500," that's 1.500; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that there as many as that. All in all, there were about 1200. It's very hard to say. We counted head up to 3- or 400 and then we stopped. There was a list but that list was never completed. In any case, there were not as many as 1500. There were fewer of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we take a look at P1280. And this is an under-seal document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What you're about to see, Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the number again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: This is an intercept from the 13th of July. And in the B/C/S, we can turn the page to see the communication between X and Y at 1602. And it starts off by saying this is mostly -- X says: "This is mostly it. I called 394. I've got an extension down in Kasaba, my own." Now 394, that was the extension used to reach Malinic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember the extension number. It was some 20 years ago. I can't say that it wasn't or that it was. It's really impossible for me to remember the extension number. I -- I don't think you should be asking me that in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, let's see if I can help you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter 05923a, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So this is the VRS phonebook. It's dated August 1995. And we have an excerpt of it at page 2. And if you look towards the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, and in the English, can you see where it says: "Commander of the Military Police Battalion," just under the heading 65th Protection Motorised Regiment. You see a phone number, and below it you see an extension, 394. Do you have any reason to dispute that this is accurate?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see where it says the battalion commander of the military police, but I don't see what commander, what battalion, and I don't see a stamp or a signature to see who was it who approved this document. But I can see all that written.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd offer 65 ter 05923a into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would object in so far as the witness is unable to authentic the information contained therein and has no personal knowledge, as he said he does not remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if documents are related to matters which are the subject of examination of the witness, we usually do not wait until -- there we have whole bunch of documents on the bar table. Is there any further objection against this to be admitted into evidence; that is, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, as to the bar table, the Prosecution has not made a submission. Pursuant to bar table jurisprudence, once we receive such submission we will respond to it in kind, but we have not received provenance information, we have not received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you know, it's not the first time, Mr. Ivetic, I think it happens very, very often, that in this context that we would decide on admission right away. So if you have any objection against admission of this document at this moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do. I've made my objection on the record. And unless the Prosecution makes any further submissions -- I cannot object in a vacuum, Your Honours. I believe Your Honours' guidance as to bar table -- I believe Your Honours' guidance as to bar table submissions has been that they should be timed prior to the conclusion of the Prosecution case. If the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, this is now the sixth or the seventh or the eighth time that you just ignore what we have done practically so often in this courtroom that if there's any document which is directly related to what a witness tell us about, that we would considered admission after having heard the parties. So you're again invited to tell us whether under Rule 87, I think it is, whether there's any objection against admission of this document. But perhaps, Ms. Hasan, if you would first tell us where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was seized in 2006 from the Kozara barracks in Banja Luka. That's part of the VRS collection -- archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it is a printed copy. It looks very much as if it is, but ... this is just print, not typewritten, or don't you know? It looks very much like print.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I -- I mean, I don't know if this is typewritten or printed. It appears to me to be printed. It was -- we actually have the entire telephone book. We've just excerpted out a page of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we saw the cover page which very much looked like not typewritten but printed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Have we received any other excerpts of this telephone book previously?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, my recollection is that I used an excerpt of this telephone book with Milenko Todorovic during his examination. I recall that I did offer that into evidence, there was a -- an objection on the basis of the date of the telephone book, and my recollection is - and I can go back and check this - that the parties agreed that this was a telephone book from August 1995 that -- as it's presented on the cover of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. Mr. Ivetic, again, if there's anything you would like to submit at this moment in relation to admission of this document before the Chamber considers whether or not to admit or even perhaps postpone its decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have nothing further to add apart from what I've already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you assign a number to the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document would receive number P7201.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Ms. Hasan, if you could provide us with the -- with the details of the information you gave us from the top of your head, then that would be appreciated. When do you think? Two days would be enough?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you feel any need to make further submissions, you have an opportunity to do so during the next two days as well. Please continue, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we go back then to P01280. And, again, this should not be broadcast. Page 2 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So the communication between X and Y continues, and X says in the third line: "Where Malinic's unit is. They said that there are 1.500 gathered at the statement [sic]." Y says: "What?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, "stadium."

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you, Your Honour. "Stadium." Y: "What?" X: "There are 1.500 at the stadium in Kasaba. Fuck it. The duty officer down there said that. We probably won't let anything get by. There are more of them ... that hasn't finished ..." And then there's some interference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can note, the B/C/S does not appear to correlate to this page. Oh, now it is. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it looks to us very much -- it is now. Witness, you can -- what was just read to you, you can read it again at the last portion of what is before you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So they're discussing the number of -- numbers gathered at the stadium where Malinic's unit is. That would be Nova Kasaba; right? That's where you were?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Nova Kasaba. And the battalion of the military police was there, I was its member. Malinic was indeed the commander of that battalion; however, I'm not familiar with this conversation. I don't know who X was, who Y was. I really can't comment upon this conversation at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The information that's being relayed between these two individuals at around 4.00 p.m., do you have -- do you have reason to dispute the numbers being reported there?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I would dispute here or what my personal opinion about this is, I don't know the situation. However, if we are talking about my battalion, about my unit, then I would dispute this number. I don't think that there were 1500 people. I'm not sure. I was there all the time. I even escorted the prisoners to Bratunac. There were about 1200 prisoners. That would be my assessment in lay terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So let's move on, then, to your escort of these prisoners. And just so that we are very, very clear: General Mladic issued the order to escort the prisoners from Nova Kasaba to the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Mladic personally issued the order to my commander. I was there when the order was being issued to him, and we complied with the order. This is exactly what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It was also General Mladic who told you -- who told you and Malinic that the buses and trucks would arrive at the football field for the transportation of those prisoners. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that in about an hour some buses were supposed to arrive. Some vehicles, some lorries. He would personally see to that and made sure that it was all organised. I don't know how he did that. In any case, he promised that the transportation means would arrive and that did happen. They, indeed, did arrive.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You understood, then, that General Mladic had ordered the organisation of the transportation for this purpose; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection. Misstates the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Hasan is not stating the evidence of the witness but she's asking a question to the witness as a follow-up to the previous question. Could you please answer the question, Mr. Subotic. The question was whether you understood that General Mladic had ordered the organisation of the transportation for this purpose, whether that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that buses would arrive. I don't know whether he issued an order to that effect, whether he approached somebody from the civilian authorities. I don't know. In any case, those were civilian buses. I was there when General Mladic promised that those buses and other vehicles should arrive within an hour and should be at the football pitch. I don't know where the information came from, whether he issued that order. He was the commander of the Main Staff, so it -- it was really impossible for me to know what the commander ordered. I was not directly subordinated to him. He was in command of the entire army. I myself was subordinated to the battalion commander who was my direct supervisor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we take look at 65 ter 32163.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, Witness, as that comes up, you recall testifying in the Popovic case as a witness for the Defence? And this was on the 1st of September, 2008.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you were called as a witness for the Beara Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You told the truth during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and again today.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So could we turn to e-court page 35, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, this is a portion -- a transcript of your testimony in that case, and I will read to you from line 9: "If I understand you well, General Mladic was the one who issued the order for the transport to be organised from Nova Kasaba to Bratunac, wouldn't that be correct? "A. Yes. And when it came to escorting prisoners of war, he was the one who issued the order, and as far as I could understand, he was the one to issue all other orders for the transport to be organised." Do you stand by the testimony you gave in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by -- by it. I repeated just a while ago that the commander of the Main Staff issued all orders. And now as to who he had arranged the transport with, I don't know that. He told us that we should escort the prisoners to Bratunac when buses and lorries arrived. I don't know who he had spoken to and made the arrangements about that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And isn't it the case, Mr. Subotic, that Mladic, General Mladic, told you in Bratunac -- told you that in Bratunac everything will be organised? Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic said that to my commander, not me. As a matter of fact, I was there. I was present. He was looking at both of us. But as a rule that order should have been issued to my commander who, in turn, should have issued the order to me. So, yes, can you interpret the whole situation as if the order had been issued to me as well because I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'm going to move onto the events or what transpired at the Nova Kasaba stadium, and you were yesterday asked about a prisoner being shot at the stadium, and the testimony is transcript page 32826. And, well, your commander Malinic was asked the same question in the Tolimir case, and I'm going to read to you his response.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we see P1555, please. And this will be e-court page 71.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And we see a question is put to Mr. Malinic about whether he had been made aware of or heard or saw any abuses of prisoners at the Nova Kasaba stadium. And in particular, whether he heard that one of the prisoners was shot and killed there at the stadium. If we turn to page 72, at line 3, Malinic provides an answer, and he says: "And as for killings, the killing of one prisoner, this is something I heard of. And it did happen at the stadium when the prisoner attacked a soldier who was a member of the Military Police Battalion." He goes on to say: "That was the only instance when someone lost his life, but it wasn't at anyone's whim. It was a question of self-defence." Now, Major Malinic heard about a prisoner being shot relating to an incidence involving a member of your police unit at the field. You must have heard of this, sir, or seen it yourself. Isn't that the truth? You were amongst those MPs at the field. Or do you claim that Major Malinic was not telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for a single moment did I say that Major Malinic was not telling the truth. The Military Police Battalion was a strong force, and I base that information on my unit of six or seven men that I commanded. This the first time I hear that a battalion of military police was -- or a military policeman was attacked by a policemen. In the Popovic case they did ask me about that murder. I don't know anything about that because there were other military policemen there from the battalion. I never heard a story like that. I can see from the document that Major Malinic also heard about that but he did not witness the situation himself. You have to ask him who he heard it from. I didn't. I've never heard before that a military policeman was attacked. I hear the first time from you. I moved around a lot on that day. I was not at the stadium all the time. I was there from the moment General Mladic arrived to the moment when the prisoners were taken away by buses and I escorted them to Bratunac. On that day, I was out on a mission with the armoured vehicle of the military police. My radius of movement was 600 metres to a kilometre. I even went to Milici to fetch bread on one occasion. That may have happened, but I really didn't hear before that a military policeman was attacked. And as for the murder you mentioned yesterday and that was mentioned to me in my last appearance before the Court, I don't know anything about that. Of my six men whose commander I was, nobody was attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you have anything more to say?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all. It is possible but I don't know anything about that. I didn't do it, none of my men did it. The police battalion was huge. Various sorts of assistance arrived on that day. You have to talk to Major Malinic and ask him who he heard that from. I never heard of an attack against the military policemen. I heard from your questions that something like that did happen. As far as I am concerned, the prisoners co-operated with me. If they hadn't, I wouldn't be sitting here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, there's no reason to tell Ms. Hasan whom she should ask a certain question. Please just answer the questions that are put to you. Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You just mentioned there were various sorts of assistance that arrived on that day. Who -- who arrived that day? Besides your unit, who was there at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about my unit, about the battalion of military police of the 65th Protection Regiment. There were four military police companies. One was an anti-terrorist component. There was a company of armoured vehicles. And our units arrived from Crna Rijeka and from all over the place to assist us. I did not have in mind all other VRS units. I just had in mind our own battalion units, all of us military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's move on. At paragraph 28 of your statement, Witness, you discuss press teams that were at the Nova Kasaba stadium, and you specifically mention one crew which you say was from the Serbian television SRNA. And you don't mention in your statement that there was, together with the military officers, who were also filming what was going on. But that's the case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that TV SRNA television, Radio Srpska. I remember that because I gave them an interview. And members of the military -- well, look members of the military. I mean, people were in uniform. I think they were from the press centre of the Army of Republika Srpska. They were carrying cameras. It's possible that they were cameramen. Probably they were since they were recording this. But what I remember is radio television of Republika Srpska from SRNA because I gave them an interview there at the stadium. That's why I remember them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And have you ever seen that recorded footage of the prisoners at Nova Kasaba or of you giving an interview? Have you ever seen that footage?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, to tell you the truth. I did ask for that. I had some friends up there, a journalist, Goran Malnaga, to go through the archives and to find this for me. However, he never managed to find that. I would really like that to happen. I'd really like to have it found. There were Muslim prisoners there too, and they confirmed everything I said during that interview. But they never managed to find that for me. Now what happened to this, I don't know. Probably it's somewhere in the archives of that television. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, we have to finish exactly in time, so therefore this would be your last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May I pose one more question and then I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, we, in our investigations, have been looking for this footage for many, many, many years, several years, and we haven't found a trace of it, either with SRNA or the VRS press centre. Do you know or have any information about what happened to this footage?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, really, I don't know. I would also like to have it found, that interview of mine because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you told us before. You say you don't know. I think that's an answer to the question, Ms. Hasan, or would you like to have any further specifics?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Only if he has more information. But otherwise, if he has no information, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You don't know anything more about that footage, where it went, in whose hands it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know. No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn for the day. And, Mr. Subotic, again tomorrow we'll start with the videolink testimony, so I'm afraid that you will have to have some more patience tomorrow as well. I don't even know whether we could resume tomorrow with you, and otherwise it would be the day after tomorrow. You'll be updated by the Victims and Witness Section. I again instruct you that you should not speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, now that the witness has left the courtroom, when you intervened and said that the question by Ms. Hasan misstates the evidence, that was an inappropriate objection. The witness who in his statement said again and again that General Mladic said that buses would arrive, et cetera, answered to one of the previous questions of Ms. Hasan showing a further commitment by saying: "... he promised that the transportation means would arrive and that did happen," and: "He would personally see to that and made sure that it was all organised." This is a commitment going further than the evidence we find in his statement. And if Ms. Hasan put a follow-up question on that, it should not have been objected to in the way you did it because that could be understood as a signal by someone that the organisation of the transportation is not what the Defence would like to hear and would misstate the evidence. It was inappropriate and inadmissible. We -- I leave it to that. We'll resume --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, objections are never admissible or inadmissible. Objections are made and are ruled upon. I take exception to your classification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They can be inappropriate. Anything done by counsel which is inappropriate - for that only reason - is inadmissible. Not in terms of criminal procedure but just something that is not acceptable, if my language is clear enough. We'll adjourn for the day. We'll resume tomorrow, 9.30 in the morning, at -- the 11th of March in this same courtroom. We stand adjourned.
